hints: Start by recalling what makes any amine basic, think about the lone pair on nitrogen and what it must do to a proton $\mathrm{H^{+}}$.
Compare ethylamine with phenylamine by asking where the nitrogen lone pair can go in each case, localised or spread into a ring.
Consider how an ethyl group pushes electrons compared with how a benzene ring and a nitro group pull electrons away.
Put the three amines in order by asking which nitrogen lone pair is most available and which is least available for bonding to $\mathrm{H^{+}}$.
walkthrough:
Fix what basic means for amines**
Picture yourself as the lone pair on nitrogen. Being basic simply means you reach out and form a dative bond to a proton, $\mathrm{R_3N: + H^{+} \rightarrow R_3NH^{+}}$. The more concentrated and available that lone pair is, the stronger the base. So every comparison here is really a comparison of lone pair availability.

Why ethylamine is the strongest**
In $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2NH_2}$ the nitrogen is attached to an alkyl group. Alkyl groups push electron density toward nitrogen by the positive inductive effect. That intensifies the negative charge on N, the lone pair is held less tightly by nothing else, and it bonds to $\mathrm{H^{+}}$ very readily. There is no ring to drain it away.

Why phenylamine is much weaker**
In $\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2}$ the p orbital containing the nitrogen lone pair overlaps with the pi system of the benzene ring. The lone pair is delocalised into the ring. It is no longer fully on nitrogen, so it is much less able to accept $\mathrm{H^{+}}$. That is why aromatic amines are far less basic than aliphatic amines.

Why the 4-nitro compound is weakest of all**
Now add a para $\mathrm{NO_2}$ group to give $\mathrm{O_2N-C_6H_4-NH_2}$. The nitro group is powerfully electron withdrawing by both inductive and resonance effects. It pulls electron density out of the ring and, indirectly, pulls the nitrogen lone pair even further away from N. The lone pair becomes even less available to bond to $\mathrm{H^{+}}$, so 4-nitrophenylamine is the least basic.

Final answer: ethylamine (most basic) > phenylamine > 4-nitrophenylamine (least basic)
Basicity depends on availability of the lone pair / p orbital on N to accept / donate to $\mathrm{H^{+}}$.
Ethyl group is electron donating by positive inductive effect, so lone pair on N in ethylamine is more available.
In phenylamine the lone pair on N is delocalised into the benzene ring, so less available.
In 4-nitrophenylamine the $\mathrm{NO_2}$ group is electron withdrawing, withdrawing the lone pair further, so least available.

hints: Look at product R, the left hand part $\mathrm{O_2N-C_6H_4-N=N-}$ must have come from Q, so ask what functional group containing $\mathrm{N_2^{+}}$ couples with a phenol.
walkthrough:
Work backwards from the azo link**
Look at R. You see $\mathrm{O_2N-C_6H_4-N=N-}$ joined to naphthol. That $\mathrm{-N=N-}$ bridge is the fingerprint of an azo dye made by coupling. The left hand $\mathrm{-N=N-}$ must have arrived as a diazonium ion, $\mathrm{Ar-N_2^{+}}$. So Q is simply the diazonium salt from 4-nitrophenylamine, with the $\mathrm{-NH_2}$ converted to $\mathrm{-N_2^{+}Cl^{-}}$, keeping the $\mathrm{NO_2}$ group para to it.
Final answer: Q is 4-nitrophenyldiazonium chloride: $\mathrm{O_2N-C_6H_4-N^{+}\equiv N\ Cl^{-}}$ with $\mathrm{NO_2}$ para to $\mathrm{N_2^{+}}$.

hints: Recall the standard way to turn a primary aromatic amine into a diazonium salt, think nitrous acid made in situ and the critical cold temperature.
Recall the conditions for the second step where a diazonium ion attacks an activated phenol, think pH needed to form phenoxide and which naphthol isomer is shown in R.
walkthrough:
Make the diazonium salt cold**
To convert $\mathrm{Ar-NH_2}$ to $\mathrm{Ar-N_2^{+}Cl^{-}}$ you need nitrous acid, $\mathrm{HNO_2}$, generated from $\mathrm{NaNO_2}$ plus excess $\mathrm{HCl(aq)}$. Diazonium salts decompose easily to give nitrogen gas, so you must keep the mixture very cold, below $10^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ in an ice bath. That is step 1.

Couple in alkali with 1-naphthol**
Diazonium ions act as electrophiles toward highly activated rings such as phenoxides. In $\mathrm{NaOH}$ solution, 1-naphthol forms the naphthoxide ion which couples rapidly at the position ortho to $\mathrm{OH}$ to give the $\mathrm{Ar-N=N-Ar}$ dye R. Alkaline conditions are essential, acid would suppress coupling.

Final answer: step 1: $\mathrm{NaNO_2}$ + $\mathrm{HCl(aq)}$ (or $\mathrm{HNO_2}$), temperature $\leqslant 10^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$
step 2: 1-naphthol in $\mathrm{NaOH(aq)}$ / alkaline solution

hints: Treat the $\mathrm{CO_2H}$ carbon as C1 of benzoic acid, then number round the ring to give the $\mathrm{NO_2}$ and $\mathrm{Br}$ substituents the lowest locants.
walkthrough:
Name from the carboxylic acid parent**
Take $\mathrm{-CO_2H}$ as the principal group, so the parent is benzoic acid with the $\mathrm{CO_2H}$ carbon as C1. Going round, $\mathrm{NO_2}$ is on C2 and $\mathrm{Br}$ is on C4. List alphabetically: bromo before nitro, giving 4-bromo-2-nitrobenzoic acid.

hints: Work backwards from G, which has $\mathrm{CO_2H}$, $\mathrm{NO_2}$ ortho to it and $\mathrm{Br}$ para to it, and remember $\mathrm{CO_2H}$ comes from oxidation of $\mathrm{CH_3}$.
Ask what F must look like if step 3 only changes $\mathrm{CH_3}$ to $\mathrm{CO_2H}$, and what E must look like if it is methylbenzene with only one of the two ring substituents added.
walkthrough:
Strip G back to the hydrocarbon skeleton**
G is a trisubstituted benzene with $\mathrm{CO_2H}$ at the top, $\mathrm{NO_2}$ ortho to it and $\mathrm{Br}$ para to it. Step 3 does not touch the ring substituents, it only oxidises the side chain. So F must be identical except with $\mathrm{CH_3}$ in place of $\mathrm{CO_2H}$: 4-bromo-2-nitro-1-methylbenzene.

Split the two ring substitutions**
E is after only one electrophilic substitution on methylbenzene. Since $\mathrm{CH_3}$ is 2,4-directing, either ortho nitration gives 2-nitromethylbenzene or para bromination gives 4-bromomethylbenzene. Either route can then add the second substituent to reach the same F, because both positions are activated by $\mathrm{CH_3}$.

Final answer: E is 2-nitromethylbenzene ($\mathrm{CH_3}$ and $\mathrm{NO_2}$ ortho) OR 4-bromomethylbenzene ($\mathrm{CH_3}$ and $\mathrm{Br}$ para)
F is 4-bromo-2-nitromethylbenzene ($\mathrm{CH_3}$ at top, $\mathrm{NO_2}$ ortho to $\mathrm{CH_3}$, $\mathrm{Br}$ para to $\mathrm{CH_3}$)

hints: Recall the classic pair of reagents that generates the nitronium ion $\mathrm{NO_2^{+}}$ for nitration of an activated ring.
Recall how bromine is made electrophilic enough to attack a benzene ring, think of the Lewis acid carrier needed.
Recall the vigorous oxidation that converts an alkyl side chain on a benzene ring fully to $\mathrm{-CO_2H}$, think hot concentrated oxidant and why heating is stressed.
walkthrough:
Nitrate with mixed acid**
Electrophilic nitration needs the $\mathrm{NO_2^{+}}$ electrophile. That is made from concentrated $\mathrm{HNO_3}$ mixed with concentrated $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$ which acts as acid catalyst and dehydrating agent. On methylbenzene this gives mainly 2-nitro and 4-nitro products, and you take the required isomer forward.

Brominate with a halogen carrier**
$\mathrm{Br_2}$ alone is not electrophilic enough for the benzene ring. Add $\mathrm{AlBr_3}$ (or $\mathrm{FeBr_3}$) as Lewis acid to polarise $\mathrm{Br-Br}$ and generate $\mathrm{Br^{+}}$ character. This gives electrophilic substitution to place $\mathrm{Br}$ ortho or para to $\mathrm{CH_3}$.

Oxidise the side chain hard**
To turn $\mathrm{Ar-CH_3}$ into $\mathrm{Ar-CO_2H}$ you need vigorous oxidation: hot alkaline $\mathrm{KMnO_4}$ with heating under reflux, then acidify to precipitate the free benzoic acid. Mild conditions stop at intermediate stages, so strong heat is essential to drive full oxidation to the carboxylic acid.

Final answer: step 1: conc. $\mathrm{HNO_3}$ + conc. $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$
step 2: $\mathrm{Br_2}$ + $\mathrm{AlBr_3}$ (or $\mathrm{FeBr_3}$ / $\mathrm{Fe}$)
step 3: hot $\mathrm{KMnO_4}$ / $\mathrm{MnO_4^{-}}$, alkaline or acidified, heat, followed by acidification
